reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Gabriella sat at the art table. She wanted to draw a rabbit. She drew one ear, but it flopped down. "My rabbit looks like a pancake," she said.

Her friend Tomo slid over a block. "Try this," he said. The block had four flat sides. Gabriella put it on her paper and traced around it. A square! She turned the square sideways. Now it looked like a body. She traced a small square for the head.

Next she found a block with three sides. She traced it twice. Two triangles stood up like ears. "Triangles have pointy tops," she said. "That is why my rabbit ears stand up now."

She traced a long block too. The rectangle made a good door for the rabbit house. Then she found a round cup. She traced the bottom. A circle made the rabbit's tail, round like a ball.

A ladybug began to crawl across her paper. Gabriella watched its round little body. She drew a tiny circle for it too.

"Look, Teacher Mia," she said. Teacher Mia smiled. "Your rabbit has square parts, triangle ears, and a circle tail. Nice work."

Gabriella held up her paper. "My rabbit can hop into his rectangle house now," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Everett ran to the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint a picture of his cute rabbit toy. The rabbit was green, his very favorite color. But there was no green paint! The pots were red, blue and yellow only. Everett looked and looked. He felt like crying.

Then he saw his friend Mia. She dipped her brush in blue paint. Then she dipped it in yellow paint too. Her paper turned green! Everett gasped. Blue and yellow made green! He grabbed his brush fast. He put blue on his paper. He put yellow on top. Green! It spread like magic.

He painted his rabbit green with big happy strokes. Then he made white snow at the bottom, like the paint was snow falling. Mia clapped. "It's so cute!" she said. Everett held up his paper and shouted, "Blue and yellow make green!"

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Avery went to the store with Mama. She saw a big red ball. Avery wanted the ball. Another girl was there too. The girl looked at the ball.

"Me first," said the girl. She hugged the ball. Avery waited. She held Mama's hand and counted. One, two, three, four, five.

The girl rolled the ball on the floor. Then she gave it to Avery. "Your turn," she said. Avery hugged the ball. It was soft like her pillow at home. It had a bright red color.

Avery rolled the ball too. Then she gave it back. "Your turn," said Avery. They took turns. Back and forth, back and forth. A worker came by. "Time to hold the ball now," she said. "No rolling in the store." So both girls held the ball.

Avery looked at Mama. "She waited, so she got a turn," Avery said. Mama smiled and nodded. The other girl waved goodbye. Avery waved back. "Bye, ball," said Avery.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Mia was ready for bed. She looked out the window. It was snowing. Soft white bits fell down, down, down. Mia felt happy. She loved snow.

Then she reached for her toy horse. It was not on the bed. Her horse was missing. Mia felt sad. She looked under the pillow. She looked under the blanket. No horse. Mia stomped her foot. She felt angry. She wanted her horse now.

Then the room went dark. A big shadow sat on the wall. Mia felt scared. She hid under the covers. "Who is there?" she asked. Daddy came in and turned on the little lamp. The shadow was just her coat. "It was my coat," Mia said. "The dark made it look big." She felt calm again.

Daddy found the horse. It was in the toy box. Mia hugged her horse tight. She felt so excited. "The snow made me look for you!" she told her horse. She snuggled down and closed her eyes. The snow kept falling outside. "Goodnight, horse," Mia said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Harrison's house. He put a big suitcase in the guest room. Grandpa unzipped it, and Harrison looked inside.

"Grandpa, why so many shirts?" Harrison asked.

"One shirt for each day," said Grandpa. "I am staying one whole week."

Harrison counted the shirts with his finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." There were seven shirts. Harrison felt a little worried. When the shirts were gone, Grandpa would go home. Each morning Grandpa put on one shirt. Each night it went in the wash basket. The pile got smaller and smaller.

Harrison had an idea. He ran to the laundry room. "Mama, help!" he said. "We wash Grandpa's shirt fast!"

Mama smiled. She washed the blue shirt. She hung it up by the window. It flapped in the air from the fan.

The next morning Grandpa picked a clean shirt from the pile. It was the blue one. "Look," said Harrison. "It came back! Washing makes it come back."

Grandpa laughed a big laugh. "Yes, it does," he said. "So I can stay my whole week."

Grandpa pulled Harrison onto his lap. His feet touched the floor on both sides, because Grandpa was so big. Harrison snuggled into the soft shirt.

"Seven days," said Grandpa. "And this is day three."

"Four more shirts," said Harrison, and he hugged him tight.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Benjamin ran to the playground. His friend Mia was on the bench. She was crying. A big dog had run by. It was too fast. It was scary for her. Now the dog was gone. But Mia was still sad.

Benjamin sat next to her. He had his toy farm in his pocket. He put the little cow in her hand. Mia stopped crying. She made the cow jump. Then she laughed.

"You are happy now," Benjamin said. "The cow made you happy." Mia nodded. They watched the little cow hop on the bench. Soon they ran to the slide together. Benjamin slid down first. Then Mia slid down too. She held the cow up high and shouted, "Whee!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Sarah sat with her family at a big table. A huge screen hung on the wall. A big game was on. Everyone looked up and watched.

But the screen had no sound. The players ran and ran. Nobody could hear the crowd. Grandpa leaned far forward. He cupped his hand by his ear. Sarah looked at the screen. Then she looked at the little box under it. A red light glowed there.

"The sound is off," Sarah said. "That is why we can't hear!" Dad smiled and pressed the button on the box. The crowd cheered loud. Everyone clapped and laughed.

A waiter came by. Dad said, "Please buy Sarah a juice. She fixed our game." The waiter brought a cold cup. Next to Sarah, a little boy dropped his spoon. "Sorry," he said. Sarah picked it up and gave it back. Then they all looked up at the screen. The players ran fast, and the crowd roared.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story: Henry ran down the hall. He was going to meet the new baby. In his pocket was a little sand from his sandbox at home. Dad stopped him at the door. "We wash our hands first," said Dad. "Sand has germs. Germs can make the baby sick." Henry looked at his hands. The sand was there, small and bumpy. Henry washed his hands at the sink. He washed slow. He washed each finger. Then Dad sat down and put a pillow on Henry's lap. "Babies are young," said Dad. "Her head is wobbly. So we hold very still." Henry held very still. Dad laid the baby on the pillow. Henry kissed her soft little head. "Hello, baby," said Henry. "My hands are clean now. That is why."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Penelope wanted to make soup for dinner. Her apron would not stay on. So she took it down from the hook where it liked to hang. Then she put it on all by herself.

"Can I help?" asked her brother Tom. He was a big boy, almost six. "Yes," said Penelope. "You can stir." Daddy put the pot on the stove. Penelope chopped an onion. Then her eyes began to water. Big tears ran down her face. She felt scared. "Why am I crying?" she asked.

Daddy gave her a hug. "The onion did that," he said. "It makes little smelly bits fly up to your eyes." Penelope sniffled. So that was it. The onion made her cry. Tom stirred and stirred, and the soup got hot. Soon the whole kitchen smelled good. "Dinner time!" called Penelope.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Felix woke up sleepy. Today was the candle party at Grandma's house. Felix wanted to hold a candle like the big kids.

The candles were in a small box. Felix tried to lift the box. It was too heavy. "Not yet," said Grandma. "Little candles need big hands."

Grandma gave Felix one candle. She lit the wick. Felix held it very still. The flame danced up high. Felix laughed. "The candle is waving at me!"

Then Felix saw it. Grandma lit her candle from Grandpa's candle. Then Dad lit his from Grandma's. The light went from one flame to the next.

"I know why," said Felix. "One fire makes many fires. Sharing makes more light!"

Grandma blew a kiss at him. Felix held his candle up high. The little flame waved back.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Grandma took Iris to the salon. Iris got a big chair. It went up and down. Her legs were too short, so she let them kick in the air. Grandma held a little card. It said "Iris, first haircut."

The hair lady came with a spray bottle. Psshh, psshh. Water fell on Iris's hair. Why water? Iris touched her hair. It was wet now. The wet hair lay flat and smooth. Dry hair had bounced up. Now the hair lady could cut it straight.

Snip, snip. Little pieces fell down. They stuck to Iris's cheek. She laughed. When the chair went down, Iris looked in the mirror. She saw short hair and a happy face. "Does wet hair cut better?" she asked. "Yes," said Grandma. "Wet hair lies flat." Iris touched her soft new hair one more time.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story: Levi stood at the running track. He held a red beanbag. A hoop lay on the ground far away. He wanted to get it in. Levi threw the beanbag high. It went past the hoop. Thump. It hit the real track floor. Why did it fly too far? Then Levi tried again. This time he swung his arm low and slow. The beanbag went up. Then it came down. It landed right in the hoop. "A slow throw goes in," said Levi. Next, his friend Mia tossed him a big ball. Levi held out one arm. The ball bounced off. Then he made a basket with both hands. The ball went right in. "Two hands catch the ball," said Levi. The kids marched around the track. Levi marched with his beanbag. What would he try next?

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Alexis visited Grandma on a rainy day. Rain went tap, tap on the window. Grandma said, "Let's find your socks. Your feet look cold."

They looked under the big chair. "One sock!" said Alexis. He held it up. It was red and soft like a bunny.

"Now we need one more," said Grandma. Alexis looked under the table. "Two socks!" he said. He counted them. "One, two, four, nine, ten!"

Grandma smiled. She touched each sock with her finger. "One, two," she said slowly. Alexis watched her fingers. He tried again. "One, two!" He put the socks on his feet. They were warm.

"It works when I touch each one," said Alexis. Grandma laughed and hugged him.

"Ten toes next," she said. "Let's count them in the tub."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Abigail could not find her bunny. She looked in the toy box. Bunny was not there. She looked behind the big chair. Bunny was not there either.

"Where are you, Bunny?" she called. Her tummy felt tight. Bunny was her real bedtime friend. She needed him for sleep.

Then Abigail had an idea. Last night she had bunny in the bed. She went to her bed. She bent down low. She looked under the bed. It was dark under there. She could not see well.

"Let me help," said Dad. He got the flashlight. He shined it under the bed. Abigail peeked again. There was bunny! "My blanket pushed him," she said. "He slid under the bed." The blanket had made bunny slide down. That is why he was hiding.

Abigail reached in and pulled bunny out. He was dusty. So she helped Dad clean him with a soft cloth. She hugged bunny close.

"Goodnight, Bunny," she whispered. She tucked him in tight. Then she slid down under her own blanket too. "Stay by me this time," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Colton ran into daycare. It was snack time soon. But today the snack was a surprise!

"I want to find the snack!" said Colton.

He used his eyes to look. He looked in the toy box. He looked under the table. No snack there. Then he used his nose to smell. He sniffed and sniffed. Something sweet! His nose smelled cookies!

Miss Maya laughed. "Good nose, Colton. Now cover your nose and try."

Colton put his hand on his nose. He could not smell the cookies anymore! He took his hand off. The sweet smell came back. His nose did the smelling. His hand made the smell stop!

"The cookies make my nose happy!" he said.

Then the cookies came out. They were warm. Colton touched one with his fingers. It was soft and a little messy on top. He took a bite. His tongue tasted sugar and chocolate.

Just then baby Ben woke up. Baby Ben heard the happy singing. His ears heard the song. He bounced in his seat.

Colton clapped. "Baby Ben hears us! I see him bounce!"

Miss Maya gave baby Ben a cookie too. He made a big messy smile.

"More cookies, more noses!" said Colton. Everyone laughed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Billie wanted to help Mama cook. The pot on the stove was hot. It made a small puff puff sound. Billie stood close to Mama, just like always. The kitchen light was bright above the counter.

Billie saw a shiny knife on the counter. "Can I hold that?" she asked. "Not that one," said Mama. "Knives are for grown-ups." Billie nodded and put her hands behind her back.

Then she saw steam rise from the pot. "What is that?" she asked. "That means it is hot," said Mama. Billie touched the cold fridge door instead. The fridge felt cool on her fingers.

"Hot pot, cold fridge," said Billie. "Steam tells me it is hot!" Mama smiled. "That's right," she said. Billie stirred the bowl Mama gave her. Then she gave Mama a big swing of her arm, and the spoon went round and round.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Hayden wants to wash his hands. His toy lion is dirty too. He carries lion to the bathroom. Mama comes with him.

Hayden sees two taps. He points to the red one. "That one is hot," says Mama. "Hot can hurt you." Hayden touches the cold tap instead. Cold water runs out. It feels nice on his fingers.

He rubs soap on lion. The water turns gray. "Lion is getting clean," says Hayden. He waits. He rinses and rinses. Slowly the soap goes away.

Then Hayden sees the little hole in the wall. Something shiny sits inside it. He wants to touch it. Mama holds his hand. "That is not for Hayden," she says. Hayden looks at the shiny thing. He looks at his clean lion.

Hayden hugs Mama's leg. "Stay close," he says. "Hot tap red. Cold tap blue." He waves the shiny hole goodbye. "Bye bye," says Hayden, and lion gets one more rinse.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Aaron rode down the big slide. He held his toy car in his hand. Then it was time for snack. Later, Aaron looked in his pocket. His car was gone.

"My car is lost!" said Aaron. His friend Mia came to help. They looked by the swings. They looked in the sand. No car. Aaron sat down on the slide steps. "I had it here," he said. "I went down the slide. Then I walked to the bench." Mia smiled. "Let me ride down the slide!" she said. Mia went down, slowly, looking left and right. At the bottom, in the green grass, something red was peeking out.

"Because you rode the same way, you found it!" said Aaron. He held his car up high. The cloudy sky turned sunny, and the two friends ran to play in the little forest of bushes by the fence, car zooming ahead.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Asher loved summer camp. His team was going to have lunch outside. But first, the camp teacher said, "Wash your hands with soap." Asher looked at the soap. He did not want to wait.

He got his bread and took a big bite. A tiny bit of dirt was on his hand. It went right onto his bread. Asher looked down. "Yuck," he said. "My bread has dirt."

The teacher smiled. "Let's try again." Asher put soap on his hands. He rubbed them while he counted. "One, two, three." He counted all the way to twenty. The bubbles felt cozy and warm.

Then he got new bread. He looked at his hands. They were clean. No dirt on the bread this time.

"Dirt gets on my food because my hands were dirty," Asher said. "So I count to twenty. Bubbles, count to twenty. Bubbles, count to twenty."

After that, Asher did not skip the sink. He washed after the toilet too. He rubbed the bubbles and counted. Then he ran to his team, holding his clean hands up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Mya went to the library storytime room. She sat on a striped cushion. The librarian read a book about a red bird. Mya clapped when the story was done.

Then the librarian said, "Mya, here is your first library card." Mya held it with both hands. It had her name on it. She picked a book about paint. It had a blue cat on the front.

"I want to keep this book forever," Mya said. "It can live in my room."

The librarian shook her head. "The book goes home with you. Then you bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Mya looked at the book. She looked at her card. She counted on her fingers. "One day, two days, three days, four days. Then I bring it back?"

"Yes," said the librarian. "You can borrow it again too."

Mya carried the book to the desk. She gave her card. The librarian stamped the book.

At home, Mya read the book to her teddy bear. She read it to her socks. She read it to her mom.

When the four days were done, Mya took the book back. A boy was waiting there. He took the blue cat book and smiled.

"The book came back," he said. "Because I brought it back," said Mya.

She picked a new book about a striped fish. "This one can come home too. Then it comes back too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Weston sat at the dinner table. He wanted the yummy bread. It sat far, far away. The bread basket was on the other side of the salt storm, where Daddy shook white salt like snow.

"Milk, please," said Mommy to Daddy. Daddy passed the milk. Weston watched with big eyes.

Weston reached for the bread. His arm was too short. He stretched and stretched. Oops. His cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table like a river.

"Sorry, Mommy," said Weston. Mommy wiped the milk. Weston thought hard. When Mommy said please, Daddy passed things. So the magic word made hands move.

"Bread, please," said Weston. Daddy smiled and passed the basket. The bread was warm and soft. Weston took a big bite. Crumbs tickled his chin.

"Thank you, Daddy," said Weston. Weston clapped his hands. The magic words worked. "Please gets bread," he said. "Thank you makes Daddy smile." Daddy gave him one more piece, just because.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Iris went to Papa's office. She saw a big tablet on his desk. She wanted to draw a monkey on it.

The screen was dark. Iris tapped it, but nothing happened. Then she found the small round button on the side. She held it down. The screen lit up. "The button makes it go on," she said.

Iris found the drawing app. It had a little paint pot on it. She tapped the paint pot. It opened. She picked a sharp pencil tool and drew a curly tail, big ears and a happy face. Then Papa said it was time for lunch.

Iris pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in its soft cover. She put it on the shelf, just like Papa showed her.

Papa printed her monkey. He gave her the page. Iris was careful, but one corner started to rip. She held the page with both hands. "Now the monkey is safe," she said. Papa smiled and pinned him up by his desk.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Isabelle went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. There were lanterns everywhere. There was a long table with little candles. The candles were for the festival of lights.

Isabelle wanted to see the candles up close. She stood on a chair. She reached out her hand. "Look, Mama," she said. "This candle is little now. It was big before!" The flame had burned the wax. The candle got short because the fire ate it. "The fire makes it small," said Isabelle. "It goes fast!"

Mama smiled. She lit a new candle. It was tall. Isabelle watched the flame. It danced and shone. The wax began to drip, drip, drip. A little drop fell onto the plate. "Another one is getting small," said Isabelle. She held Papa's hand and watched the light.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story: Emmett went to the store with Dad. Emmett wanted to make pizza for dinner. He picked a red apple, but Dad said, "We need cheese and bread." Emmett put cheese in the cart. He put round flat bread in the cart, too. At home, Emmett began to build his pizza. First the sauce. Then the cheese on top. Mom put the pizza in the hot oven. Emmett waited. He watched the little window. The cheese was hard and cold before. Now it went soft and bubbly. "The hot oven melts the cheese," said Emmett. Water dripped off the lettuce and made a puddle on the floor. Emmett wiped it up slowly with a towel. Ding! The pizza was ready. Emmett took a big bite. "Tasty!" he said. "More cheese, please, Emmett," said Mom, holding out her plate.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Gabriel wanted the big red truck. His sister Mia had it. She held it tight in her hands.

"One more minute," said Mom. "Then it is your turn." Mom set the timer. It went tick, tick, tick. Gabriel watched it. How did the timer know? At school, his teacher used a timer too. The timer said beep! Mia gave him the truck.

"Your turn," she said. "Thank you, Mia," said Gabriel. He pushed the truck. Vroom, vroom. Mia waited and waited. She did not grab it. The timer went tick, tick, tick again. Beep! Now it was Mia's turn.

"Can we share?" asked Gabriel. He put blocks in the truck. "You put them in. I dump them out," said Mia. They both laughed. Then Gabriel had an idea. He tickled the truck like a baby? No! He tickled Mia's toes instead. She laughed so big.

"The timer helped us," said Gabriel. "We both got turns." Mia hugged the truck tight, then she hugged Gabriel too. "Tick, tick, beep!" she shouted.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Norah wants to bake a cake. The cake's name is Big Sun Cake. Norah mixes eggs, milk and flour in a shiny silver bowl. She stirs and stirs. The batter is smooth and wet.

Norah pours the batter into a pan. She puts the pan in the oven. Then she waits. She waits some more. Nothing happens. The batter stays wet and cold.

Mom smiles. "The oven is not on yet," she says. Mom turns the dial. A little light glows. The oven gets hot. Hot, hot, hot.

"Now watch," says Mom. The batter puffs up. It gets big and round like a real sun. Norah claps her hands.

"The oven was cold," says Norah. "Cold ovens do not bake. Hot ovens bake cakes!"

Dad comes in. "Stop, my tummy is growling," he says with a grin.

Norah cuts him the first big piece.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. She had ten little peas on her plate. She wanted to count them all by herself.

"One, two, three," said Iris. She pushed one pea with her finger each time. "Four, five, six." Then she stopped. The next word was hiding from her. "Eight?" she said. Dad shook his head and smiled.

Dad held up seven fingers, no, just some fingers, near her plate. "Sss," he said, like a soft snake. "Seven!" said Iris. She poked the next pea. "Seven! Then eight, nine, ten." All the peas had a number. The clock on the wall gave a little tick. Iris ate one pea. "Now nine!" she said. Dad laughed and ate one too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Penelope went to the store with Mama. She held her toy monkey, Mo. Mo had a low bump on his head. "Mo is hungry," said Penelope. "What do monkeys eat?" Mama smiled. "What do you think?" Penelope thought hard. "Bananas! Monkeys eat bananas!"

First they walked down the toy aisle. There were balls and blocks and a big red truck. Penelope looked high. She looked low. No bananas here. "This is the toy aisle," she said. "Toys are for playing. Bananas are food!"

So they walked to the food part of the store. There were apples and bread and milk. And there, on a low shelf, sat a big yellow bunch of bananas. Penelope reached up. She picked one out. "Mo, look! A banana for you!" She held it near Mo's mouth. "Mmm," she said, in her best monkey voice. "Yum, yum, yum."

Mama laughed. "Mo likes it here." Penelope hugged the banana and Mo together. At home, Penelope ate the banana herself. Mo watched from the table. "Monkeys share," Penelope told him. Then she took a crayon and tried to write the word banana, but she only made a wiggly line. "That says banana," she said. Mo seemed happy. "Mmm," said Penelope, in her best monkey voice again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Jacob ran to the big slide at the playground. He touched it. "Ouch! Why is it so hot?" he asked. The sun was shining on it all day. That was why.

So Jacob ran to the small slide. It sat under a tree, in the shade. He touched it. It felt cold. "Ha! The sun makes the big slide hot," Jacob said. "The shade keeps the small slide cold."

Jacob slid down the small slide. He went slow. Then he slid down the big, hot slide very fast. "Whee!" Fast and slow. Hot and cold. Big and small.

A boy named Tom laughed. "You went down the smelly slide," he teased. "A dog sat on it!" Jacob giggled and held his nose. "Yuck!"

Then Jacob got to ride the twisty merry-go-round. Round and round he went, fast, then slow, then fast. "This is my best gift ever," he said. "A sunny day at the playground!"

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jake put on his clean blue shirt. Grandma made it for him. It smelled like warm soap.

At school, Jake built a tall block tower. It was very tall. Ben bumped the table. The tower fell down. Crash. Jake felt sad. His eyes got wet.

"Ben, you bumped the table," said Jake. "The tower fell because of the bump." Ben felt bad. "I am sorry," he said. "I will help you."

Then Ms. Kim rang the little bell. "Story time!" she said. Jake felt excited. He loved stories. He jumped up and down. Ben laughed.

Ms. Kim read a book about a bear. "Can you spell bear?" she asked. "B, E, A, R," said Jake. He felt happy.

Ben and Jake built the tower again. It was even taller. "This tower is so big!" said Jake. He gave Ben a big hug.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
The bookmobile came to Edouard's street. It was a little truck full of books. Edouard climbed the steps with his mom.

The library lady smiled at him. "Would you like your own card?" she asked. Edouard nodded. He got a card with his name on it. He picked a book about a big red truck.

He held the book tight. "Can I keep it forever?" he begged.

"Not forever," said the lady. "You can take it home. Then you bring it back by a certain day. Other people want to read it too."

Edouard looked at the book. Other kids liked trucks too. Maybe someone else was waiting for this one.

"Can I read it tonight?" he asked. "And bring it back next time?"

"Yes," said the lady.

That night, mom read the book to him twice. Edouard fell asleep with the truck book under his pillow.

The next morning he asked, "Is it the bring-back day yet?"

Mom laughed. "Not yet, little one. First we read it some more."

Edouard smiled and turned the page.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Sara ran to the park with Daddy. Her bunny was gone! Bunny was lost somewhere.

"Where did you play last?" asked Daddy. Sara thought hard. "The sand!" she said. "Bunny was in the sand!" They ran to the sand box. Not here. Look again! They ran past the water cup fountain. Not here. Look again! A big dog began to bark, bark, bark at a thin green bush.

Sara peeked in the bush. No bunny. Then she remembered. She had sat on the bench for a snack. They ran to the bench. Sara bent down low. She looked under it. There was bunny, soft and sandy, waiting by her shoe!

"I found you!" Sara hugged bunny tight. The dog barked one happy bark, as if to say hello.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Lucy sat at her big table. She wanted to paint her doll's dress green. She looked and looked. "Where is the green paint?" she asked. There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. No green.

"Cat, do you see green?" she asked. The cat said, "Meow." Lucy laughed. "Silly cat. You see naps."

Lucy had an idea. She put one drop of blue in a cup. She put one drop of yellow in the cup. She stirred it round and round. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said. "The blue did it. The yellow helped."

Outside, it began to snow. The snow fell on the grass. "Look, Cat!" said Lucy. "The deep snow hides the green grass." She painted the doll's dress. It was green, green, green.

"Now you have a green dress," Lucy told the doll. The cat said, "Meow."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Logan had a little drum. He wanted to play a song. He hit the drum very fast. The sounds came out all jumbled. The cat ran under the chair.

"This is hard," said Logan.

Mama sat down next to him. She showed him the drum. "Try it slow," she said. "Slow and steady."

Logan hit the drum. Bump. Bump. Bump. He went slow. The bumps sounded nice. The cat came back and sat by his feet.

Logan went slow, one, two, three. Then he went slow some more. Then he tried a little faster. Bump-bump-bump! The song came out just right.

"I did it!" said Logan. "Slow made it work. Fast made it messy."

Mama clapped her hands. Logan patted the cat. The cat purred very soft.

"Play it again," said Mama. So Logan read his drum book, found a new song, and began to play. Bump. Bump. Bump.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Aurora went to the dentist with her mama. The chair was big. It had a wheel on one side. "Can I spin it?" she asked. "Yes, but only once," said Dr. Kim.

Dr. Kim had a little mirror. "Open your mouth wide," she said. Aurora opened it very wide. She was a young girl, but she could open like a lion. "Roar," said Dr. Kim, and Aurora giggled.

Then Aurora closed her lips. The mirror could not see her teeth. "Oh no," said Dr. Kim. "My mirror is sad." Aurora opened again. The mirror went in. "I see the problem. A spot is hiding." Dr. Kim let the water squirt wash it away. "The spot went away because I opened my mouth!" said Aurora. "That's right," said Dr. Kim. "Now let me spin the chair wheel once."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Isabella put on her red shoes. Today was a school day. At school, Mr. Tom had a chart. "Ben feeds the fish today," said Mr. Tom. Isabella wanted to feed the fish too. "When can I feed them?" she asked. "Tomorrow," said Mr. Tom. Isabella made a sad face. Tomorrow felt very far away.

Then Isabella watched the day. Now it was story time. Later it was snack time. Then the sun went low in the sky. Mom came to pick her up. "Sleep first," said Mom. "Then tomorrow comes."

Isabella slept in her high bed. She woke up. The sun was high again. She put on her red shoes. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom, smiling.

At school, Isabella got the little cup of food. She fed the fish. The fish ate fast. "Yesterday Ben fed you," she said. "Today I feed you!"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
It was Saturday morning at Charles's house. Everyone came to watch the big game. Papa sat on the couch. Aunt Jo sat on the floor. Uncle Ben sat by the door. Charles counted the people. "One, two, three, four, and me makes five!"

The red team ran with the ball. Then the red team scored. Everyone jumped up and shouted. The shout was loud. It felt scary to Charles. He hid behind Papa's leg. "It is okay," said Papa. "I am right here."

Charles watched again. The blue team ran with the ball. The blue team did not score. Nobody shouted. Charles looked around. He saw why the shouting happened. "They shouted because the red team scored," he said. Papa smiled and nodded. Aunt Jo dropped some chips. She had to sweep them up with her hand. Then the red team scored one more time. Everyone shouted again. This time Charles shouted too. "Go red team!" said Charles. Papa gave him a big hug.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The whole room went dark. Leo's mama lit some candles. The candles made little flames. The flames made big shadows on the wall.

"Look!" said Leo. He moved his hand near a candle. His shadow moved too. He wiggled his fingers. The shadow fingers wiggled. "It moves because of the light!" he said.

The flashlight was on the table. Leo grabbed it. He clicked it on. But the light was small and dim. He clicked it again. Still dim. "The battery is low," said Mama. "We are a team. You hold the candle. I will hold this one."

The flame tickled the air above it. Leo giggled. "The candle is tickling!" he said. The wax began to drip down the side. Mama said bedtime would come early tonight.

Leo held his candle all the way to his room. His shadow walked with him, big on the wall. "Come on, shadow," said Leo. "Sleep time."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Gabriel was at Grandma's house. Grandma waved from the porch. "Come see, Gabriel," she said. Gabriel ran to the big table. Grandma had paper and paints. "We will make a map," she said. "A map for a treasure walk."

Gabriel drew a tree on the map. But he wanted green paint for the leaves. There was no green pot on the table. There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. Gabriel frowned. "No green," he said.

He dipped his brush in the yellow pot. He made a yellow leaf. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue pot. The yellow leaf turned green. Gabriel opened his eyes wide. "Yellow and blue make green!" he said. He painted more green leaves, one by one.

Then they walked the map to the treasure. It was a jar of salty crackers by the red door. A blue bird sat on top. "Crunch," said Gabriel. Grandma laughed and waved to the bird.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Luca sat in the car with his blanket. It was soft and white. Mama was in the front seat. They were going to get the new baby.

Luca held up his blanket. "This is for the baby," he said. "Babies like big kid things."

Mama smiled. "Babies are very small," she said. "They cannot hold a big blanket yet."

At the house, Daddy put the baby in Luca's arms. Luca gave the blanket. The baby's hands did not grab it. The blanket fell down. Luca picked it up.

Then Luca tried a little sock. The baby grabbed the sock! One little hand held on tight.

Luca counted, "One sock, two hands, three little fingers." The baby held the sock all the way home.

Luca whispered, "Babies like little things. I will bring little things." The baby squeezed the sock again.
